Put every channel on a linear scale and find the top of its range

Source: R/read-fcs.R
linearise_channels.Rd

WHY. An analog instrument with log amplifiers (a FACSCalibur, for one) stores integer channel numbers 0 to $PnR - 1 on a log scale, and $PnE f1,f2 declares it: f1 decades, offset f2. Every transform this package fits assumes linear intensity, so an arcsinh or logicle laid over channel numbers puts a log on top of a log and moves every valley. FCS 3.1 allows log storage only for integer data (Spidlen et al. 2010).

Usage

linearise_channels(ex, kw, label = "")

Arguments

ex

Expression matrix, events x channels, in file order.

kw

FCS keywords.

label

File name for the log line.

Value

list(exprs, scale), scale a data.frame with one row per channel: f1, f2, stored ("linear", "log, linearised" or "log declared on floats, used as stored"), range (top of scale in the units now held, or NA) and margin_at (the value at and above which an event is at the margin, or NA).

Details

WHAT. Integer channels with f1 > 0 are converted to f2 * 10^(f1 * x / $PnR), with f2 = 0 read as 1, which is exactly what flowCore's read.FCS(transformation = "linearize") computes. Their range becomes f2 * 10^f1.

FLOATING-POINT DATA WITH A NON-ZERO $PnE breaks the standard, and the values are not converted, because flowCore does not convert them either and nothing says what scale they are on. flowCore's own GvHD example, written back out with write.FCS(), is like this: linear floats up to 10,000 under the FACSCalibur keywords $PnE 4,0 and $PnR 1024. The $PnR of such a channel describes the original channel numbers rather than the stored values, so it is not used as the channel's range. Capping those values at 1024 is what put a pile of identical values in the middle of the demo cohort's CD45 data.
